questions.question: In a standard Transformer encoder block, what are the primary roles of self-attention, the position-wise feed-forward network (FFN), and layer normalization?
questions.choice_A: Self-attention mixes information across tokens via content-dependent weights; the FFN applies token-wise nonlinear transformations to expand modeling capacity; LayerNorm stabilizes training by normalizing per-token feature statistics.
questions.choice_B: Self-attention provides positional information; the FFN aggregates across tokens; LayerNorm regularizes by randomly zeroing features.
questions.choice_C: Self-attention increases model depth; the FFN compresses sequence length; LayerNorm enforces sparsity.
questions.choice_D: Self-attention only handles local context; the FFN handles global context; LayerNorm prevents vanishing gradients by scaling weights.

questions.question: Why are pre-norm Transformer architectures (LayerNorm applied before attention/FFN sublayers) often favored for very deep models?
questions.choice_A: They reduce the number of parameters without changing depth.
questions.choice_B: They improve gradient flow across many layers, making optimization more stable without extensive warmup or careful initialization.
questions.choice_C: They allow removal of residual connections entirely.
questions.choice_D: They eliminate the need for learning rate schedulers.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts Vision Transformers (ViTs) with convolutional backbones regarding linear transformations?
questions.choice_A: ViTs avoid all linear layers and rely solely on attention, whereas CNNs use only convolutions.
questions.choice_B: CNNs and ViTs both rely on shared spatial weight tying in their linear projections.
questions.choice_C: ViTs use a learned linear projection for patch embedding and MLPs applied identically per token, while CNNs use spatially local, weight-shared filters that implicitly encode translation equivariance.
questions.choice_D: ViTs use fixed random features for patch embedding, while CNNs learn fully connected layers at each pixel.

questions.question: What is a typical high-level pipeline for text-to-image diffusion models used in practice?
questions.choice_A: Tokenize text, run an autoregressive Transformer to produce pixels directly, and apply a VAE for post-processing.
questions.choice_B: Encode text into a one-hot vector, feed to a GAN generator, then denoise with a UNet.
questions.choice_C: Encode text with a CNN, generate a segmentation mask, and fill with a texture synthesizer.
questions.choice_D: Encode text with a pretrained text encoder, iteratively denoise latent variables with a conditional UNet guided via cross-attention and a scheduler, then decode latents to pixels with a VAE decoder.

questions.question: Where do linear transformations commonly appear in text-to-image diffusion systems?
questions.choice_A: In attention projections (Q/K/V/O) and 1x1 convolutions within the UNet, in the VAE encoders/decoders, and in the text encoder’s embedding and projection layers.
questions.choice_B: Only in the final pixel-space convolutional layer after denoising.
questions.choice_C: Exclusively inside the scheduler, which is responsible for linearizing the diffusion process.
questions.choice_D: Only in the classifier-free guidance mechanism.

questions.question: When applying parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) like LoRA to large Transformers, which placement is typically most effective?
questions.choice_A: Only in the embedding layer to directly change tokenization.
questions.choice_B: Insert low-rank adapters on attention projection matrices (Q, K, V, and output) and optionally in MLP projections, while keeping LayerNorms and most base weights frozen.
questions.choice_C: Replace all LayerNorms with trainable batch norms to increase capacity.
questions.choice_D: Train only the final linear classifier head across all tasks.

questions.question: What is a key trade-off between using a single shared adapter across all Transformer layers versus separate per-layer adapters?
questions.choice_A: Shared adapters always outperform per-layer adapters because they impose more regularization.
questions.choice_B: Per-layer adapters use fewer parameters but are less expressive than a shared adapter.
questions.choice_C: Shared adapters reduce parameter count and storage across tasks, but may bottleneck representation capacity since different layers learn different functions; per-layer adapters better capture layer-specific transformations at higher parameter cost.
questions.choice_D: There is no practical trade-off; both approaches are equivalent if trained long enough.

questions.question: In what scenario is prefix/prompt tuning often preferred over adapters or LoRA for conditioning large language or diffusion backbones?
questions.choice_A: When full finetuning of all base weights is computationally cheap.
questions.choice_B: When you need to drastically change the model’s tokenization scheme.
questions.choice_C: When the deployment forbids any additional parameters at inference time.
questions.choice_D: When you want to avoid modifying base weights and keep per-task parameter overhead and memory footprint minimal by learning small key-value or prompt vectors.

questions.question: What does activation (gradient) checkpointing do in order to reduce memory usage during training?
questions.choice_A: Stores only a subset of intermediate activations and recomputes the missing ones during backpropagation, trading extra compute for lower memory.
questions.choice_B: Eliminates the need to store gradients by using second-order optimizers.
questions.choice_C: Compresses activations with lossy quantization during the forward pass.
questions.choice_D: Caches entire model states on CPU between steps.

questions.question: Why is bfloat16 (BF16) often preferred over float16 (FP16) for mixed-precision training of very large models?
questions.choice_A: BF16 has more mantissa bits, so it is always more precise than FP32.
questions.choice_B: BF16 has a wider exponent range comparable to FP32, reducing underflow/overflow and often removing the need for dynamic loss scaling.
questions.choice_C: BF16 requires half the memory of FP16.
questions.choice_D: BF16 guarantees identical results across all GPUs without seeding.

questions.question: In memory-efficient distributed training, what does ZeRO Stage 3 specifically shard or partition to enable larger models?
questions.choice_A: Only optimizer states, leaving gradients and parameters replicated.
questions.choice_B: Only gradients, leaving parameters and optimizer states replicated.
questions.choice_C: Optimizer states, gradients, and parameters are all partitioned across data-parallel ranks.
questions.choice_D: Only activations are partitioned across pipeline stages.

questions.question: How does gradient accumulation help maintain a target global batch size under memory constraints, and what is a practical caveat?
questions.choice_A: It increases the learning rate while decreasing the batch size, which always improves generalization.
questions.choice_B: It reduces the number of optimizer steps per epoch, which always speeds up convergence.
questions.choice_C: It halves the memory by skipping the forward pass for some microbatches.
questions.choice_D: It sums gradients over multiple smaller microbatches before an optimizer step to emulate a larger global batch; however, optimizer dynamics and learning rate schedules may need retuning rather than naive linear scaling, especially with adaptive optimizers.

questions.question: For finetuning text-to-image models, which data pipeline considerations most directly affect downstream quality and stability?
questions.choice_A: Caption quality and consistency, near-duplicate removal, resolution bucketing with appropriate resize/crop augmentations, and careful tokenization/truncation handling.
questions.choice_B: Using deterministic shuffling only, avoiding any augmentations, and removing all punctuation from captions.
questions.choice_C: Minimizing dataset size to avoid overfitting regardless of domain.
questions.choice_D: Randomly mixing text-only corpora with images without captions.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when creating validation splits for finetuning vision or multimodal models on web-scale data?
questions.choice_A: Including too many classes in the validation set reduces variance.
questions.choice_B: Near-duplicates leaking from train to validation can inflate metrics; hashing-based deduplication and stratified splitting help ensure a clean and representative validation set.
questions.choice_C: Using fixed random seeds always prevents any leakage.
questions.choice_D: Shuffling batches before splitting eliminates class imbalance.

questions.question: Which evaluation approach best reflects the goals of text-to-image alignment rather than only image realism?
questions.choice_A: Rely exclusively on Inception Score since it measures diversity and quality of generated images.
questions.choice_B: Use pixel-wise MSE between generated and ground-truth images for all prompts.
questions.choice_C: Complement FID with alignment-sensitive metrics such as CLIPScore or retrieval-based precision/recall, plus targeted human evaluations for faithfulness and safety.
questions.choice_D: Only inspect training loss curves for convergence.

questions.question: Which pattern in training and validation curves most strongly indicates overfitting during finetuning, and what is a standard response?
questions.choice_A: Both training and validation metrics improve steadily; increase learning rate.
questions.choice_B: Validation loss decreases while training loss increases; reduce batch size.
questions.choice_C: Training loss oscillates; switch to SGD without momentum.
questions.choice_D: Training loss continues to decrease while validation loss stops improving or worsens; consider early stopping, stronger regularization, or reduced training budget.

questions.question: For Vision Transformer finetuning with adapters, where should parameter-efficient modules typically be inserted to balance capacity and efficiency?
questions.choice_A: After the self-attention and after the MLP sublayers (within the residual blocks), while keeping the patch embedding and positional encodings largely frozen for compatibility.
questions.choice_B: Only at the very end of the network before the classifier head.
questions.choice_C: Inside the softmax of attention to alter normalization.
questions.choice_D: Replace all MLPs with convolutional layers.

questions.question: When adapting a latent diffusion model to a narrow domain with limited compute, which finetuning strategy is generally effective?
questions.choice_A: Train the VAE from scratch but freeze the UNet to preserve generalization.
questions.choice_B: Freeze most of the UNet and VAE while applying low-rank adapters to attention projections (and optionally some MLPs) in the UNet, possibly adjusting the text encoder minimally or keeping it frozen.
questions.choice_C: Double the number of diffusion steps and train only the scheduler.
questions.choice_D: Remove classifier-free guidance to simplify optimization.

questions.question: Which statement about computational load in Transformer blocks is generally accurate for large models?
questions.choice_A: Self-attention dominates FLOPs, while FFNs are mostly memory-bound and cheap.
questions.choice_B: The output projection in attention accounts for nearly all compute.
questions.choice_C: FFNs often dominate FLOPs due to the expansion ratio (e.g., 4\times hidden), while attention can be more memory- or bandwidth-bound; optimizing GEMMs and fusing activations in FFNs yields substantial speedups.
questions.choice_D: Layer normalization accounts for the majority of training time.

questions.question: What is a robust protocol for reporting finetuning results to ensure fair comparison and reproducibility?
questions.choice_A: Report the single best run, omit hyperparameters to keep the method proprietary.
questions.choice_B: Use only validation performance for model selection and publish that as the final test metric.
questions.choice_C: Tune hyperparameters on the test set to avoid overfitting the validation set.
questions.choice_D: Fix random seeds when appropriate, control nondeterminism where possible, log and release code/configs/checkpoints, evaluate on a held-out test set, and report mean and variance over multiple seeds or runs.

questions.question: In large-scale mixed-precision training, which practice helps maintain numerical stability without sacrificing throughput?
questions.choice_A: Disable all normalization layers to reduce precision issues.
questions.choice_B: Use BF16 or carefully managed FP16 with dynamic loss scaling, keep critical operations (e.g., LayerNorm, softmax, reductions) in FP32, and employ fused kernels for common patterns.
questions.choice_C: Quantize all weights and activations to 8-bit during both forward and backward passes.
questions.choice_D: Replace AdamW with a second-order optimizer to avoid scaling problems.
